name: Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda; the Mādhva sampradāya)
alt_names: Brahma-sampradāya (its place in the later scheme of four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas)

tradition.text: the tradition traces the teaching to Nārāyaṇa (as Haṃsa) through Brahmā and a line of teachers; Vyāsa (an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa) fixed it in the Brahmasūtras; in the Kali age Madhva, the third avatāra of Vāyu, re-proclaimed it

scholarly.text: founded by Madhva in the 13th c. CE; living

transmissions_received.what: the Brahmasūtras as the root text, commented on by Madhva
ten principal Upaniṣads, read as teaching difference and Viṣṇu's supremacy
the Pañcarātra accepted as valid scripture (sadāgama); mantra and worship lore
the Mahābhārata and the Gītā as scripture of the highest rank
Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas insofar as they agree with the sadāgamas
authorless Veda, intrinsic validity, the marks of purport (upakrama etc.) — adapted
debate theory and logical vocabulary — adopted in part and criticized

transmissions_given.what: Dvaita doctrine (Hari's supremacy, gradation of souls) sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas, several of them disciples of Mādhva ascetics (Śrīpādarāja, Vyāsatīrtha, Vādirāja)
the Gauḍīya tradition claims descent from Madhva's line through Mādhavendra Purī; the claim is disputed (see brw:dvaita-gaudiya-parampara)

distinctive_positions: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa, Hari) alone is independent (svatantra); Lakṣmī, all souls, matter, time and the Veda are dependent (paratantra) on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1; Tattvaviveka 1).
Five real and eternal differences (pañca-bheda) — God–soul, God–matter, soul–soul, soul–matter, matter–matter — hold in every state, including liberation (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 1.68–71).
The world is real (satya); the Advaita doctrines of māyā, the world's falsity (mithyātva) and the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) are refuted (the ten prakaraṇas; Nyāyāmṛta).

Souls are innately graded (tāratamya) and fall into three classes — fit for liberation (mukti-yogya), ever-transmigrating (nitya-saṃsārin), fit for blinding darkness (tamo-yogya); a soul's fitness is beginningless and unalterable (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 4–7; MBTN 1.86–95).
Liberation is the soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss, graded even among the liberated (ānanda-tāratamya), in eternal difference from and dependence on Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu is full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of every defect; 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities; his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are not different from him (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 3).
Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge there is no abundant grace (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.1).
Bhakti is firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness (MBTN 1.85); it continues in liberation as eternal bliss (MBTN 1.104).

Three means of valid knowledge — perception, inference, authoritative word; perception is sevenfold, the witness (sākṣin) plus six senses; what the sākṣin establishes is never sublated (Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Anuvyākhyāna).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa) is the highest of souls; grace descends through the higher beings; Madhva is Vāyu's third avatāra after Hanumān and Bhīma (MBTN 32.162–166).
God is the efficient cause of the world, not its material cause; prakṛti is the material cause.

All words, letters and scriptures in their primary sense designate Viṣṇu; the Veda is authorless; valid scripture (sadāgama) is the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas that agree with them (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God — dependent on and similar to its original (bimba), and eternally distinct from it.
Chāndogya 6.8.7 is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), taught nine times with examples to show difference (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
summary: The Vedānta school founded by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called by its adherents Tattvavāda, 'the doctrine of reality'. It teaches that Viṣṇu alone is the independent reality, that souls and matter are real, dependent and eternally distinct from him and from one another (the five differences), that souls are innately graded, and that liberation — the soul's enjoyment of its own bliss in Viṣṇu's presence — comes only by his grace, won through knowledge and devotion. Its classical literature runs from Madhva's thirty-seven works through Jayatīrtha's commentaries and Vyāsatīrtha's polemics to Rāghavendra; it is carried by ascetic maṭhas (the eight of Uḍupi with their biennial rotation of Kṛṣṇa worship, and the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) and was sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas.
notes: The tradition's teacher line before Madhva (the 'Haṃsa paramparā': Haṃsa-Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the Sanaka group, Durvāsas, then a line of ascetics ending in Acyutaprekṣa) is recalled here only in outline; the intermediate names are not listed because they were not verified in this pass. A traditional verse likens the doctrine to a tree: seed sown by Vyāsa in the soil of śruti, sprouted by Madhva, branched by Jayatīrtha, leaved by Vyāsarāja, flowered by Vijayīndra and fruited by Rāghavendra (quoted as a preface verse in a modern edition in the raw_etexts corpus; author not identified). Further maṭhas (Śrīpādarāja maṭha at Mulbagal, Subrahmaṇya, Bhīmanakaṭṭe, Bhaṇḍārakeri; the Gauḍa Sārasvata Mādhva maṭhas of Kāśī and Gokarṇa-Partagāḷī) are mentioned without separate entries — details not verified.

name: Kashmir Śaivism (non-dual Śaiva tantra of Kashmir)
alt_names: Trika (in the broad sense used by Abhinavagupta and modern writers)
Īśvarādvayavāda (Utpaladeva's name for the non-duality of the Lord, Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti ch. 2)
regions: Jālandhara (seat of Abhinavagupta's Kaula teacher Śambhunātha)
South India / Cola country (Maheśvarānanda's Krama, c. 1300)

tradition.text: The Śaiva scriptures issue from Śiva's five faces; after they were lost at the start of the Kali age, Śiva as Śrīkaṇṭha commissioned Durvāsas to restore them (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-111); the Śiva Sūtras were revealed to Vasugupta on Mahādeva mountain.

scholarly.text: c. 850 CE (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa) - 11th c. classical period (Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, Kṣemarāja); commentarial and devotional continuation to the 18th-19th c.; revived in the 20th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhairava tantras (Svacchanda, Netra, Mālinīvijayottara, Siddhayogeśvarīmata) as scriptural base; the 36 tattvas, the three malas, śaktipāta and dīkṣā
transmissions_received.evidence: Kṣemarāja's Svacchandoddyota and Netroddyota; Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka built on the Mālinīvijayottara (TĀ 1.18)

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual and the kula/akula doctrine, via Śambhunātha of Jālandhara
transmissions_received.evidence: Tantrāloka 29; TĀ 5.52 (the seven ānandas as taught by Śambhu[nātha])

transmissions_received.what: Bhartṛhari's doctrine of speech (vāc) and pratibhā, reworked as vimarśa = supreme speech
the epistemological framework and vocabulary of Dharmakīrti's school, engaged polemically

transmissions_given.what: prakāśa-vimarśa metaphysics and Spanda/Pratyabhijñā exegesis used by Śrīvidyā commentators (e.g. Jayaratha's Vāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa; Maheśvarānanda)
Abhinavagupta's aesthetics (rasa as relished consciousness; śānta rasa)
the oral and textual lineage continued in the 20th c. by Swami Lakshmanjoo

distinctive_positions: Reality is one consciousness (saṃvit, citi), Paramaśiva, whose nature is light (prakāśa) inseparably joined with reflexive awareness (vimarśa); an awareness without vimarśa would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).

The world is a real manifestation (ābhāsa) of that consciousness by its own freedom (svātantrya), displayed on its own screen (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 2) - not an illusory appearance (Advaita's vivarta) and not a separate matter.

Bondage is the contraction of consciousness through the three impurities; the root impurity is ignorance, not a substance (TĀ 1.22-23 citing the Mālinīvijayottara); liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Śiva.
Knowledge (jñāna) is the sole cause of liberation; ritual and yoga are means graded to the recipient's grace.
The thirty-six tattvas (Śiva to earth), extending Sāṃkhya's twenty-five with the pure principles and the five kañcukas.
Four means (upāya): anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava - graded by the intensity of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) with full activity in the world; the liberated sees the world as his own play.
Śiva performs five acts (emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace); the bound individual also performs them (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 10-11).
Spanda: the ultimate is dynamic vibration, the opening and closing of Śaṅkara's eyes (Spandakārikā 1.1).
Kaula ritual, including its antinomian elements, is interpreted by Abhinavagupta as an expression and means of non-dual consciousness (TĀ 29) - summary only.
summary: The non-dual Śaiva exegetical tradition of Kashmir (9th-11th c. classical period) that interpreted the Bhairava and Kaula tantras (Mālinīvijayottara, Svacchanda, Netra, Vijñāna Bhairava, Parātrīśikā) through four interlocking systems - Spanda (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa), Pratyabhijñā (Somānanda, Utpaladeva), Trika (culminating in Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka) and Krama (the Kālī-centred Mahānaya) - with the Kula and the little-known Mata alongside. It teaches that the self is Śiva, the world his free self-manifestation, bondage a contraction and liberation its recognition, attained by four graded means. Continued by Kṣemarāja, Jayaratha, the Kashmiri devotional poets (Lal Ded, Rūpa Bhavānī, Sāhib Kaul) and, recently, Swami Lakshmanjoo.
notes: 'Kashmir Śaivism' is a modern umbrella name; the tradition itself speaks of Trika, Ṣaḍardha, Pratyabhijñā, Spanda, Krama, Kula. Parent set to the Mantramārga because its scriptures are Bhairava tantras of the Mantramārga; its Kaula side derives from the Kulamārga (lin:kaula).

name: Krama (the 'Sequence'; Mahānaya, Mahārtha)
regions: Oḍḍiyāna (in the tradition's account of Jñānanetra's revelation)

tradition.text: Revealed by the goddess to Jñānanetra (Śivānanda) - the tradition's account.

scholarly.text: Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala etc.) before c. 900; Kashmirian Krama c. 850-1000; Maheśvarānanda c. 1300; Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa later.

transmissions_received.what: the Kālīkula scriptures and the cult of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī

transmissions_given.what: the twelve Kālīs integrated as a form of śāktopāya (TĀ 4.148-172)
Krama ideas in Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī, which also draws on Śrīvidyā

distinctive_positions: Worship and contemplation of Kālī as the power that 'counts', emits and devours (kalana) all things; the five senses of the root kal: projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).

The twelve Kālīs as the phases of every act of cognition - emission, persistence, withdrawal and the nameless (anākhya) - across object, means of knowledge and knowing subject (TĀ 4.148-172; Abhinavagupta's Kramastotra).
The five flows (pañcavāha) of goddesses: Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī, Bhūcarī (low confidence).
Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, 'she who draws in time', is supreme.
The sequence (krama) of cognition leads into the sequenceless (akrama).
summary: The Kālī-centred Kaula tradition of the northern transmission as practised in Kashmir (Mahānaya, Mahārtha), rooted in the Jayadrathayāmala and related Kālīkula scriptures and said to have been revealed to Jñānanetra. Abhinavagupta absorbed its doctrine of the twelve Kālīs into the Trika (TĀ 4; Kramastotra); Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī and Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa are later statements. Much of its scripture survives only in manuscript or citation.
notes: Parent set to the Kashmirian grouping; historically a Kālīkula (lin:kalikula) Kaula system.

name: Mata (the 'Doctrine'; the Mata scriptures)
regions: Kashmir (as known to Abhinavagupta and Jayaratha)

scholarly.text: Known only through references by Abhinavagupta (c. 1000) and Jayaratha (13th c.); origin and dates unknown.

distinctive_positions: Its scriptures (mataśāstra) reject the samaya observances and similar rules as based on difference, teaching instead that one's own awareness, unbounded and complete, is to be realized (TĀ 4.262-263 with Jayaratha, who quotes the Mata line 'nirmaryādaṃ svasambodhaṃ sampūrṇaṃ budhyatām').
They forbid restricting eating and the worship of the cakra to members of one's own lineage (santāna), because such division fragments the undivided reality (TĀ 4.268-270).

In the Kashmirian scriptural hierarchy the Mata stands between the Dakṣiṇa (right-hand Bhairava) scriptures and the Kula (TĀ 13.300-301 and the verse quoted there by Jayaratha); a variant verse quoted in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa places it after the Kula and just below the Trika.
summary: A Śaiva/Kaula scriptural tradition, now lost, that the Kashmirian exegetes count as one of the systems alongside Kula, Krama and Trika. What is known comes almost entirely from the Tantrāloka and Jayaratha's Viveka: its rejection of the samaya rules and of lineage-based exclusions, and its rank in the scriptural hierarchy. Its own texts, deities and teachers are not securely identified in this skeleton.
notes: Low confidence throughout. Jayaratha on TĀ 4.262 calls the Mata scriptures 'samaviṣamalakṣaṇa' - sense unclear. Modern scholarship (Sanderson) associates the Mata with a Kālīkula/northern-transmission cult; that identification is not asserted here and is listed as a gap.

name: Pratyabhijñā (the philosophy of recognition)

scholarly.text: Somānanda c. 900-950; Utpaladeva c. 925-975; Abhinavagupta's Vimarśinī dated Laukika 90 (c. 1014/15 CE); Kṣemarāja c. 1000-1050.

transmissions_received.what: the logical-epistemological idiom of Dharmakīrti's school, answered polemically
the idea that awareness is intrinsically verbal (vāc); critique of paśyantī as ultimate

distinctive_positions: Liberation is the recognition that one's own self is the Lord (Īśvara), endowed with the powers of knowing and acting; the Lord cannot be proved or denied since he is the ever-established knower (ĪPK 1.1.2-3).
Consciousness is essentially reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), 'supreme speech arising of itself', and this is the Lord's freedom and sovereignty (ĪPK 1.5.13-14).

Memory, cognition and exclusion (jñāna, smṛti, apohana) are possible only if a single conscious subject contains the diverse within itself (ĪPK 1.3.7, 1.4.3) - against the Buddhist denial of an enduring self.
Objects are manifestations (ābhāsa) of consciousness shown as if external by the power of māyā.
The ultimate is not the grammarians' paśyantī (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1ff.).
Devotion (bhakti) is the enjoyment of the identity with Śiva already recognized (Utpaladeva's Śivastotrāvalī).
summary: The philosophical school founded by Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi) and systematized by Utpaladeva (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his two commentaries), commented on by Abhinavagupta and summarized by Kṣemarāja (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya). It argues, in dialogue with Buddhist logicians, grammarians, Naiyāyikas and Vedāntins, that the individual can recognize himself as Maheśvara, and that this recognition itself is liberation.

name: Rāghavendra Maṭha (Mantrālaya)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha whose pontiffs included Surendra Tīrtha, Vijayīndra Tīrtha (Kumbhakonam), Sudhīndra Tīrtha and Rāghavendra Tīrtha; since Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya on the Tuṅgabhadrā (1671) the seat and pilgrimage centre have been there.
notes: Its descent from Madhva via the Kavīndra Tīrtha line and a later division (Vibudhendra Tīrtha) is recorded at low confidence.

name: Spanda (the doctrine of vibration)

tradition.text: The Śiva Sūtras were revealed to Vasugupta on Mahādeva mountain - in a dream by Paramaśiva who showed him a rock that turned over at his touch (Kṣemarāja, Śivasūtravimarśinī intro.), or 'by a siddha's command' (Bhāskara, Śivasūtravārttika 1.3).

scholarly.text: c. 850-900 CE (Vasugupta and Kallaṭa; Kallaṭa is placed under King Avantivarman, 855-883, by the Rājataraṅgiṇī); commentaries to Kṣemarāja (c. 1000-1050) and later.

transmissions_given.what: the Spanda texts were read together with Pratyabhijñā by Kṣemarāja
Spanda doctrine is a pillar of Abhinavagupta's and Kṣemarāja's Trika

distinctive_positions: The ultimate is Śaṅkara, from whose opening (unmeṣa) and closing (nimeṣa) of the eyes the world arises and dissolves; this dynamic pulsation is spanda (Spandakārikā 1.1).
The knowing and acting subject never ceases through waking, dream and deep sleep; what is lost in sleep is only the effort turned to objects, not the inner agent (SK 1.3, 1.14-16).
Spanda can be grasped in intense states - great anger, joy, perplexity, running - and at the gap where one thought ends and another arises (SK 1.22, 3.9).
Bondage comes from the powers arising from the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) when they are not recognized; recognized, the same power grants perfection (SK 3.13-16).
'Consciousness is the self; knowledge [limited] is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.1-2); 'effort is Bhairava' (1.5).
The Śiva Sūtras are read (by Kṣemarāja) as teaching the three means in three sections: śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava.
summary: The earliest systematic current of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism, founded on the Śiva Sūtras revealed to Vasugupta and the Spandakārikā (ascribed to Vasugupta by Kṣemarāja, to Kallaṭa by Rāmakaṇṭha, Bhagavadutpala and Bhāskara). It presents the ultimate as vibrant, self-aware power (spanda), identical with one's own agency, discoverable in every moment of intense experience, and absorbed later into the Trika synthesis.

name: Trika ('the Triad')

tradition.text: Revealed by Bhairava; the Mālinīvijayottara presents itself as taught by Kārttikeya to the sages (MVT 1.1-7).

scholarly.text: Trika scriptures of the Vidyāpīṭha (Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Mālinīvijayottara) c. 6th-9th c.; exegetical Trika of Abhinavagupta c. 990-1020; Jayaratha 13th c.

transmissions_received.evidence: TĀ 1.18: the essence of the Lord's scripture is Trika, its essence the Mālinīvijaya

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual and doctrine (the Kaula form of Trika)

distinctive_positions: The triad of goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā with Bhairava; in Abhinavagupta's Trika Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī stands above them as the fourth.
The triads Śiva-Śakti-Nara (aṇu), icchā-jñāna-kriyā, and non-difference, difference-in-non-difference, difference.
The Trika is the essence of all Śaiva scripture and the Mālinīvijayottara is the essence of the Trika (TĀ 1.18).
Scriptural hierarchy: Veda < Śaiva (Siddhānta) < Vāma < Dakṣiṇa < Mata < Kula < Kaula < Trika (verse quoted by Jayaratha on TĀ 13.301; TĀ 13.300-301 grades śaktipāta in the same order).
Four means of immersion (samāveśa): anupāya (TĀ 2), śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava (MVT 2.21-23, TĀ 1.168-170).
Phonematic emanation: the letters as mātṛkā (A to KṢA) and in the scrambled order mālinī (NA to PHA); the Heart (hṛdaya) as the seed of the universe (Parātrīśikā 24).
summary: The 'Triad' tradition: a Vidyāpīṭha cult of the goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā grounded in the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and Mālinīvijayottara, which Abhinavagupta made the frame of his synthesis of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism in the Tantrāloka and Tantrasāra, incorporating Kaula, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā. It ranks itself highest among Śaiva revelations.

name: The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi (aṣṭa-maṭha)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: Eight monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Madhva for eight of his ascetic disciples, who worship in turn the image of Kṛṣṇa that Madhva installed at Uḍupi: Palimaru (Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha), Adamaru (Narasiṃha Tīrtha), Krishnapura (Janārdana Tīrtha), Puttige (Upendra Tīrtha), Shirur (Vāmana Tīrtha), Sode (Viṣṇu Tīrtha, Madhva's brother), Kaniyooru (Rāma Tīrtha) and Pejavara (Adhokṣaja Tīrtha). The worship rotates among them (paryāya); the tradition credits Vādirāja Tīrtha of Sode with changing the turn from two months to two years (from 1522).
notes: The maṭhas are paired (Palimaru–Adamaru, Krishnapura–Puttige, Shirur–Sode, Kaniyooru–Pejavara) — recorded from memory, moderate confidence. The two-monthly original rotation and the 1522 date should be checked.

name: Uttarādi Maṭha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: One of the three principal Mādhva maṭhas (with the Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas). It traces its pontiffs from Madhva through Padmanābha Tīrtha, Narahari Tīrtha, Mādhava Tīrtha and Akṣobhya Tīrtha to Jayatīrtha and Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha; its later pontiffs include Raghūttama Tīrtha, Satyanātha Tīrtha and Satyadharma Tīrtha, most taking names beginning with 'Satya-'. It venerates Jayatīrtha's brindāvana at Malkheḍ.
notes: The division of the line after Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha (Kavīndra Tīrtha's line leading to this maṭha and, after a later split, to the Rāghavendra maṭha; Rājendra Tīrtha's line leading to the Vyāsarāja maṭha) is recorded here from memory at low confidence. The 'Mūla Rāma' images held by the tradition to have been brought from the Kaliṅga treasury by Narahari Tīrtha are claimed by this maṭha and the Rāghavendra maṭha — not verified.

name: Vyāsarāja Maṭha (Sosale)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha of Vyāsatīrtha (Vyāsarāja), disciple of Brahmaṇya Tīrtha; seated at Sosale (Mysuru district). Vyāsatīrtha's brindāvana is at Nava Brindāvana near Ānegondi (Hampi).
notes: Its descent from Madhva through Rājendra Tīrtha, Jayadhvaja, Puruṣottama and Brahmaṇya Tīrtha is recorded from memory at low confidence.
